WFP Burkina 
May 2026 
Contact info: Liam Wylie (liam.wylie@wfp.org) 
Country Director: ai Aline SAMU (aline.samu@wfp.org) 
 
WFP BURKINA FASO 
COUNTRY BRIEF 
May 2026 
KEY HIGHLIGHTS 
• In April, WFP assisted 415,351 people, delivering 
3,590 mt of food. This reflects a slight decrease 
compared to March, mainly due to operational 
constraints, while efforts continued to reach 
vulnerable populations. 
• Humanitarian needs remain significant, 
underscoring the importance of sustained 
assistance to protect vulnerable populations and 
consolidate recent gains. 
• WFP continues an integrated response across 
food assistance, nutrition, school meals and 
resilience, requiring USD 99.6 million for May–
October 2026 to sustain operations and avoid 
further deterioration in food security. 
IN NUMBERS

Photo Caption & Credit: WFP/Photographer Jecuthiel Yameogo 
 
SITUATION OVERVIEW 
 
• Burkina Faso faces a complex crisis driven by 
insecurity, climate shocks, and structural 
vulnerabilities. Reliance on rainfed agriculture 
heightens exposure to climate variability. Insecurity 
remains the primary driver of humanitarian needs, 
with 2 million internally displaced persons (latest 
official figure, March 2023), limiting access to land, 
markets, and essential services. 
• The preliminary results from the April 2026 national 
food security and nutrition analysis projects 1.66 
million people will face crisis-level food insecurity (IPC 
Phase 3+), including 223,000 people in emergency 
situations, during the June–August 2026 lean season, 
compared to 2.3 million in 2025. While the situation 
shows an overall improvement relative to last year, 
access constraints remain significant in several 
regions, despite localized progress observed in 2025 
such as the restoration of access to Titao and 
Barsalogho. 
• Already in 2025, funding shortfalls forced WFP to 
reduce its coverage by around 30 percent compared 
to 2024, contributing to deteriorating food 
consumption and increased negative coping 
strategies among vulnerable households. WFP 
continues to deliver an integrated response including 
emergency food and nutrition assistance, school 
feeding, resilience activities, and common services 
through UNHAS, supporting national efforts toward 
stabilization and food sovereignty.
WFP Burkina Faso Country Brief 
May 2026 
OPERATIONAL UPDATES 
General Food Assistance 
• In April, WFP distributed over 2,907 mt of food and 
nutrition assistance to 197,404 people in localities 
such as Silmague, Seguenega, and Diapaga, 
including 180 mt airlifted to localities such as 
Kantchari or Gorgadji. 
• WFP took part in two government-mandated 
convoys: one to Gayeri and another to Sebba and 
Solhan. WFP had last joined convoys to these 
locations in April 2025 and December 2024, 
respectively. 
• The main challenge remains funding constraints, 
which limit WFP’s ability to meet needs. In addition, 
two WFP airlift helicopters were unavailable due to 
operational and administrative constraints, 
significantly reducing airlift capacity and increasing 
reliance on road transport. 
Nutrition 
• WFP supported malnutrition prevention by 
assisting 855 young children and 553 women, while 
screening over 2,600 children and identifying very 
few cases of moderate malnutrition; nutrition 
awareness reached more than 4,300 people. 
• To treat moderate acute malnutrition, WFP 
provided specialized nutritious foods to over 
31,700 children and 15,600 women. 
• WFP also strengthened local production of fortified 
foods through quality audits and training for 
national producers, improving standards and 
capacity. 
School-Based Assistance 
• In April, WFP reached 236,644 students (56 percent 
girls) with daily hot meals in 755 schools, including 
7,259 students who received take-home rations 
(THR), to support attendance and retention. 
• Under the integrated programme, 171,950 
students (56 percent girls) in 629 schools received 
hot meals, with THR provided to upper primary 
students meeting attendance criteria. Under 
emergency school feeding, 64,694 students (54 
percent girls) in 126 schools were assisted, 
including 34,484 IDPs, with support limited to on-
site meals due to funding constraints. 
• Efforts focused on programme quality and capacity 
strengthening (field monitoring, partnerships, 
kitchen construction), alongside coordination with 
partners and government, including Education 
Cluster engagement and planning for the phase-
out of emergency school feeding by end-2026. 
Resilience and Livelihood Support 
• In April 2026, WFP strengthened community 
resilience through the Food Assistance for Assets 
(FFA) programme, supporting the production of 
185 compost heaps (9 m³ each), treatment of 17 
gullies, and restoration of 86 hectares of degraded 
land. Activities also included the construction of 
2,101 improved cookstoves, rehabilitation of 14 
water ponds, seedling production, and assistance 
to 2,686 beneficiaries with 266 mt of food. 
• Through the Smallholder Agricultural Market 
Support (SAMS) programme, WFP reinforced 
livelihoods by supporting farmer organization 
targeting and delivering SBCC messaging, while 
strengthening capacities through trainings of 40 
participants (13 women) on GBV/PSEA and data 
collection, alongside project staff induction and 
technical workshops. 
United Nations Humanitarian Air Service 
(UNHAS) 
• In April 2026, UNHAS supported humanitarian 
operations through 246 flights to 27 destinations, 
serving 71 user organizations, and transporting 
1,351 passengers as well as 22.9 mt of light cargo. 
Despite limited flight cancellations, UNHAS 
maintained access to isolated and hard-to-reach 
locations, including Bourzanga, Gorgadji, Arbinda, 
Djibo, and other remote areas. 
 
FUNDING OVERVIEW 
Country Strategic Plan (2019-2026) 
 
 
Donors: 
Donors to WFP’s Burkina Faso Country Strategic Plan include 
Austria, Burkina Faso, Canada, Denmark, the European 
Commission, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, 
Luxembourg, Monaco, the Netherlands, Norway, the Republic 
of Korea, the Russian Federation, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, 
the United Kingdom and the United States of America. 
Additional support was provided by the UN Central Emergency 
Response Fund (CERF) and private donors, including the Ajram 
Foundation, Buddhist Global Relief, the Gwendolyn Sexton 
Foundation, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day 
Saints.

Displacement levels continue to decline, with the proportion of displaced persons residing in collective shelters decreasing from 11 per cent to 9 per cent over the past two weeks.

related.excerpt: Situation Report Lebanon Crisis 23 June - 7 July 2026 Highlights The humanitarian situation in Lebanon remains fragile despite a reduction in hostilities, with significant and persistent humanitarian, protection, and early recovery needs. Daily airstrikes and military operations, particularly in southern Lebanon, continue to pose risks to civilians and limit safe returns, highlighting the potential for renewed escalation despite ongoing diplomatic efforts. Since 2 March 2026, a reported 4,304 people have been killed and 12,203 have been injured. Women and girls are bearing the brunt of the crisis, facing heightened protection and gender-based violence (GBV) risks, disrupted health services, including for maternal health, and reduced access to safe and dignified support. Since the onset of the crisis, UNFPA has reached over 150,000 displaced people with sexual and reproductive health (SRH) and GBV services. related.title: South Sudan at 15: A humanitarian journey through conflict, resilience and hope
related.summary: Fifteen years on, humanitarian needs continue to grow South Sudan became the world's youngest nation in July 2011 with hopes of a more peaceful future. During the first half of 2026, surgeries at Juba Military Hospital increased by nearly 30 per cent compared with the same period last year, leaving the ICRC-supported surgical department operating at more than 100 per cent capacity. At the same time, arrivals of people fleeing conflict in neighbouring Sudan and declining humanitarian funding are placing additional strain on already overstretched services.
bullets: Fifteen years on, humanitarian needs continue to grow South Sudan became the world's youngest nation in July 2011 with hopes of a more peaceful future.

During the first half of 2026, surgeries at Juba Military Hospital increased by nearly 30 per cent compared with the same period last year, leaving the ICRC-supported surgical department operating at more than 100 per cent capacity.
At the same time, arrivals of people fleeing conflict in neighbouring Sudan and declining humanitarian funding are placing additional strain on already overstretched services.
For the ICRC, remaining alongside these communities has meant adapting to changing humanitarian needs while maintaining one constant priority: protecting lives and preserving human dignity.

During the first six months of 2026, the ICRC evacuated 266 wounded patients from conflict-affected areas across South Sudan, an increase of more than 50 per cent compared with the same period in 2025.
related.excerpt: As South Sudan marks 15 years of independence, millions of people continue to live with the consequences of conflict and violence. For more than 40 years, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has worked alongside communities across the country, helping people survive conflict, recover from injury and rebuild their lives. Through these moments captured over the years, we look back at that journey and the humanitarian needs that continue today. Fifteen years on, humanitarian needs continue to grow South Sudan became the world's youngest nation in July 2011 with hopes of a more peaceful future. Fifteen years later, many communities continue to face the daily consequences of conflict and violence as well as climate-related shocks. The humanitarian situation has become even more challenging in recent months. Renewed fighting since late 2025 has forced thousands of families from their homes, disrupted livelihoods and reduced access to health care. At the same time, arrivals of people fleeing conflict in neighbouring Sudan and declining humanitarian funding are placing additional strain on already overstretched services. related.title: Malawi Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027: Crisis (IPC Phase 3) anticipated in the south through January driven by weather shocks (pdf)
related.summary: FEWS NET estimates that 1.5-1.99 million people will require humanitarian food assistance during the October- January lean season. While plans for humanitarian assistance have not yet been finalized, past trends indicate that assistance is typically provided from November through at least January, coinciding with the peak of the lean season. Below-average rainfall is likely in southern Malawi during the 2026/27 season, with October to January rains delayed and poorly distributed.
bullets: FEWS NET estimates that 1.5-1.99 million people will require humanitarian food assistance during the October- January lean season.

While plans for humanitarian assistance have not yet been finalized, past trends indicate that assistance is typically provided from November through at least January, coinciding with the peak of the lean season.
Below-average rainfall is likely in southern Malawi during the 2026/27 season, with October to January rains delayed and poorly distributed.

Above-average food prices, combined with atypically low agricultural labor opportunities, are expected to constrain poor households’ ability to access food through market purchases, leading to food consumption gaps.

However, the southern region of Malawi, including the Southern Lakeshore, Middle Shire, and Lower Shire Livelihood Zones, experienced below-average harvests due to dry spells and flooding during the main rainy season.
related.excerpt: Crisis (IPC Phase 3) anticipated in the south through January driven by weather shocks Key Messages Malawi - Food Security Outlook June 2026 - January 2027 Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected in parts of southern Malawi (the area of highest concern) and localized areas of the central region from October 2026 through January 2027, a marked deterioration following widespread Minimal (IPC Phase 1) and Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes through September. These outcomes will likely be driven by the early depletion of household food stocks following below-average 2026 harvests and reduced purchasing power. Above-average food prices, combined with atypically low agricultural labor opportunities, are expected to constrain poor households’ ability to access food through market purchases, leading to food consumption gaps. Stressed (IPC Phase 2) outcomes are expected across the remaining southern districts and several central region districts over the same period, as households are likely to meet minimum food needs but cannot afford some non-food expenditures without engaging in negative coping strategies.
